sample.universe: All individuals registered as residents of the Copenhagen urban agglomeration (NUTS-3 areas Byen Kobenhavn and Kobenhavns omegn, 17 municipalities) in 2007, 2011 or 2014; the area had 1.26 million inhabitants in 2014
selection_rules: registered as a resident of one of the 17 municipalities in the calendar year
individuals who died or emigrated during a year, or who have missing addresses, are excluded
regression samples are restricted to non-immigrants (natives and descendants of immigrants); separate models are run for natives and for descendants

sample.period: 2007, 2011 and 2014, with 2003 data used to compute the 2003-2007 change in neighborhood composition
sample.n_observations: 2,517,583 person-years in the descriptive sample (2,369,115 excluding all missing values): 811,418 in 2007, 836,702 in 2011, 869,463 in 2014 (Table 2)

construction_notes: Neighborhoods are individualized and scalable: each individual's neighborhood is their k nearest neighbors, k = 800 for the local neighborhood and k = 51,200 for the extralocal neighborhood, computed with EquiPop from 100 x 100 m grid coordinates
Most individuals have their k = 800 nearest neighbors within the first three rings of grid cells, i.e. within a radius of 300 m

Minority group: immigrants and descendants of immigrants originating from countries outside Europe (excluding Turkey), North America and Oceania; two alternative groupings (non-Western; predominantly Muslim country of origin) are used in supplementary analyses

Neighborhood educational level: share of individuals aged 25-64 who have completed tertiary education; neighborhood affluence: share of people aged 25-64 with taxable income in the highest decile of the national income distribution
Change in the local minority concentration is computed between 2003 and 2007, 2007 and 2011, and 2011 and 2014
Out-migration is coded by comparing the residential grid cell on 1 January and on 31 December of year t

Six individual-level control variables plus year dummies are used: three broad age groups (25-44, 45-64, 65+), sex, marital status, number of children (childless, 1-2, 3+), educational attainment (low/medium/high) and current employment
Wealth, homeownership and housing tenure are not available in the data set and are not controlled for

claims.statement: Among non-immigrants (natives and descendants) in Copenhagen, a higher share of visible minorities among a person's 800 nearest neighbors raises the odds of moving to a different grid cell during the year.

treatment.label: Proportion of visible minorities among kNN 800

definition.value: The local concentration of minorities: the share of minority individuals in the focal individual's individualized, scalable neighborhood consisting of the k = 800 nearest neighbors, computed with the EquiPop software from 100 x 100 m residential grid coordinates. A minority individual is an immigrant or a descendant of immigrants originating from countries outside Europe (excluding Turkey), North America and Oceania.

timing.value: measured in the same year as the outcome (2007, 2011, 2014)

outcome.label: Out-migration (moved to a new 100 x 100 m grid cell during the calendar year)

definition.value: Binary indicator of whether an individual changed place of residence during calendar year t, constructed by comparing the 100 x 100 m residential grid cell on 1 January and on 31 December of year t; different codes are coded as an out-migration event. Individuals who died or emigrated during the year, or who have missing addresses, are excluded.

timing.value: during calendar year t, for t = 2007, 2011 and 2014

units.value: logit coefficient b (change in the log-odds of out-migration) for the regressor as scaled in the paper; the table also prints the corresponding odds ratio OR = 2.49

magnitude.interpretation: 'A one standard deviation higher share of minorities is associated with approximately a two-and-a-half-fold increase in the odds of out-migration (b = 0.912, odds ratio (OR) = 2.49) when controlling for individual and neighborhood characteristics.' (p. 180)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: once the two neighborhood socioeconomic controls, the individual-level controls and the year dummies are included, the remaining association between neighborhood minority concentration and out-migration is not driven by further common causes. The authors motivate the controls as a way to 'avoid confusing the effects of the environment with the effects of individual characteristics', and concede the control set is not comprehensive.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. The authors state the opposite in their limitations: the control set 'is by no means comprehensive, and other factors ... may drive our results'.

ambiguities: Models 1-3 in the same table are nested specifications of the same relationship; this claim records Model 3, the fullest specification, which the paper interprets in the text. In Model 1 (no controls) the coefficient on the change in the minority share is large and negative in every panel (e.g. -4.431*** in the Full panel) and turns positive only once controls are added, so the sign of that regressor is specification-dependent.

The paper reads the coefficients as effects of a one-standard-deviation change in the minority share, while Table 3 reports the neighborhood composition variables as proportions; whether the regressors were standardized is not stated.

evidence.how: Table 2 reports the mean of the out-migration indicator over the pooled descriptive sample of all residents (natives 0.826, immigrants 0.161, descendants 0.013). The Full-panel regression excludes immigrants, so 0.117 is the closest printed baseline rate for this outcome but is not exactly the estimation sample's mean.

ambiguities: Models 1-3 in the same table are nested specifications of the same relationship; this claim records Model 3, the fullest specification, which the paper interprets in the text. In Model 1 (no controls) the coefficient on the change in the minority share is large and negative in every panel (e.g. -4.431*** in the Full panel) and turns positive only once controls are added, so the sign of that regressor is specification-dependent.

The paper reads the coefficients as effects of a one-standard-deviation change in the minority share, while Table 3 reports the neighborhood composition variables as proportions; whether the regressors were standardized is not stated.
